paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive intellectual developmental disorder-43 (MRT43) is a disorder of intellectual disability. It was first reported as nonsyndromic intellectual disability. Later reports described motor problems, including clumsiness, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and dysarthria, and syndromic presentations with dysmorphic features, macrocephaly or microcephaly, skeletal anomalies, and skeletal muscle involvement. Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that the phenotype is heterogeneous.

paragraphs.text: Assoum et al. (2020) reported 3 patients with syndromic intellectual disability. Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules. The younger sister also had congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. The third patient was 34 years old and had mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly. Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that the gene is responsible for a heterogeneous autosomal recessive intellectual disability phenotype and that more case descriptions would be needed to refine it.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from 7 children who were homozygous for the WASHC4 P1019R mutation. These were the patients originally reported by Ropers et al. (2011), and their data had been obtained in 2010 at the Royal Hospital in Muscat, Oman. Developmental delay or learning difficulties were the main reason for medical evaluation, but all patients also had motor symptoms (mean age, 10.4 years). On clinical examination their movements were described as 'clumsy,' with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. The children were by then an average of 21 years old, and recent communication with their parents revealed no notable worsening of symptoms.

paragraphs.text: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, Ropers et al. (2011) combined homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing. After SNP filtering, only 2 changes remained. One was a homozygous nonsynonymous change in the SWIP (WASHC4) gene, which the authors considered causative because of its high pathogenicity and conservation scores and on functional grounds. The mutation significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and endosomal transport. Courtland et al. (2021) identified this mutation as c.3056C-G (P1019R) and noted that cell lines from the patients had decreased amounts of WASH proteins.

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) proposed a mechanistic model based on their findings in a mouse model (see ANIMAL MODEL). In this model, SWIP P1019R causes loss of WASH complex function, which disrupts the endo-lysosomal system. Over time this leads to accumulation of neurodegenerative markers, including unfolded protein response modulators, lysosomal enzymes, lipofuscin, and cleaved caspase-3, resulting in cognitive deficits and progressive motor impairment. The authors noted that the human P1019R mutation has not been classified as a neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL). However, findings in the mutant mice, including lipofuscin accumulation, suggested that loss of WASH complex function leads to phenotypes strongly resembling the NCLs. In mouse brain, they identified a neuronal WASH proteome of 175 significantly enriched proteins using in vivo BioID with a WASH1 probe. It included all 5 WASH complex components, 13 known WASH interactors, and proteins with endosomal, endocytic, cytoskeletal, and postsynaptic functions, supporting a major role for the WASH complex in endosomal trafficking in brain.

checks.claim: The lysosomal module increased in Washc4 P1019R mutant mouse brain contained cathepsins, hydrolases such as HEXA, GBA, GLB1, MAN2B1, and MAN2B2, and progranulin.
checks.evidence_quote: M36 (Figure 4B) contained several lysosomal cathepsin proteases (CTSA, CTSB, CTSS, and CTSL) as well as key lysosomal hydrolases (HEXA, GBA, GLB1, MAN2B1, and MAN2B2)
checks.explanation: Progranulin (GRN) is also stated to be in M36.

checks.claim: Cultured cortical neurons from Washc4 P1019R mutant mice had larger somatic EEA1-positive early endosomal puncta than wildtype neurons, with no change in their number.
checks.evidence_quote: MUT neurons display larger EEA1+ somatic puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5G and J), but no difference in the total number of EEA1+ puncta

checks.claim: Cultured cortical neurons from Washc4 P1019R mutant mice had fewer but larger cathepsin D-positive lysosomal puncta than wildtype neurons.
checks.evidence_quote: MUT neurons exhibited significantly less Cathepsin D+ puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5H), but the remaining puncta were significantly larger than those of WT neurons

paragraphs.text: At 10 months of age, mutant mice had significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining, selectively in motor cortex (44.01% vs 25.38% of nuclei); this increase was not present at adolescence. Electron microscopy of motor cortex from 7-month-old mutant mice showed electron-dense lipofuscin deposits that were increased in size and number. Behaviorally, mutant mice performed normally in novel object recognition and the Y-maze. However, they had a persistent deficit in cued fear memory recall at both adolescence and adulthood, with intact responses to footshock and tones. They also had progressive motor dysfunction: rotarod retention was reduced by nearly 50% at both ages, and gait abnormalities (longer swing time, longer strides, and reduced homologous coupling) emerged in adulthood.

checks.claim: At 10 months of age, Washc4 P1019R mutant mice had significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining selectively in motor cortex (44.01% vs 25.38% of nuclei).
checks.explanation: Values match, and difference was selective for motor cortex.

checks.claim: Increased cleaved caspase-3 staining was not present in Washc4 P1019R mutant mice at adolescence.
checks.evidence_quote: No difference is seen at P42, but the amount of CC3+ nuclei is significantly higher in aged MUT mice

checks.claim: Electron microscopy of motor cortex from 7-month-old Washc4 P1019R mutant mice showed electron-dense lipofuscin deposits increased in size and number.
checks.evidence_quote: the marked increase in lipofuscin area and number seen in MUT electron micrographs (Figure 6O and P, respectively)
checks.explanation: TEM at 7mo motor cortex; size and number increased.

checks.claim: Washc4 P1019R mutant mice performed normally in novel object recognition and the Y-maze.
checks.evidence_quote: MUT mice performed equivalently to WT mice in episodic and working memory paradigms, including novel object recognition and Y-maze alternations

checks.claim: Washc4 P1019R mutant mice had a persistent deficit in cued fear memory recall at both adolescence and adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: Additionally, this deficit in fear response was evident at both adolescence and adulthood

checks.claim: Washc4 P1019R mutant mice had intact responses to footshock and tones.
checks.evidence_quote: In line with intact sensation, MUT mice responded comparably to WT mice in these tests
checks.explanation: Startle to footshock and tones were intact.

checks.claim: Washc4 P1019R mutant mice had progressive motor dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: These findings demonstrate that SWIPP1019R results in progressive motor function decline

checks.claim: Rotarod retention in Washc4 P1019R mutant mice was reduced by nearly 50% at both adolescence and adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: At both ages, the MUT mice exhibited an almost 50% reduction in their ability to remain on the rod

checks.claim: Gait abnormalities (longer swing time, longer strides, and reduced homologous coupling) emerged in Washc4 P1019R mutant mice in adulthood.
checks.evidence_quote: MUT mice took slower (Figure 8E), longer strides (Figure 8F), stepping closer to the midline of their body (track width, Figure 8—figure supplement 1), and their gait symmetry was altered
checks.explanation: Gait parameters were indistinguishable at adolescence and altered at 5.5mo (longer swing time, longer strides, decreased homologous coupling).

clinical_synopsis.feature: congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic intellectual disability, Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsynonymous change in the WASHC4 (SWIP) gene. The mutation significantly reduced SWIP levels and destabilized the entire WASH complex.

checks.claim: Ropers et al. (2011) studied affected members of a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive nonsyndromic intellectual disability.
checks.evidence_quote: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID), we have combined homozygosity mapping
checks.explanation: The title specifies the disability was non-syndromic.

checks.claim: Ropers et al. (2011) used homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing to identify a homozygous nonsynonymous change in the WASHC4 (SWIP) gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we have combined homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment and high-throughput sequencing to identify the underlying gene defect. After appropriate single-nucleotide polymorphism filtering, only two molecular changes remained, including a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP
checks.explanation: The methods and the non-synonymous SWIP change are stated. Homozygosity is inferred from the homozygosity-mapping design.

checks.claim: The WASHC4 (SWIP) mutation identified by Ropers et al. (2011) significantly reduced SWIP levels.
checks.evidence_quote: we could show that this mutation leads to significantly reduced SWIP levels

checks.claim: The WASHC4 (SWIP) mutation identified by Ropers et al. (2011) destabilized the entire WASH complex.
checks.evidence_quote: this mutation leads to significantly reduced SWIP levels and to destabilization of the entire WASH complex

paragraphs.text: Courtland et al. (2021) identified this mutation as a homozygous c.3056C-G transversion in the WASHC4 gene, resulting in a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution, and studied 7 children from the family reported by Ropers et al. (2011), whose data had been obtained in Oman. All had developmental delay or learning difficulties and motor symptoms, including clumsiness, fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria. In HEK cells, mutant SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wildtype SWIP. Mice carrying the corresponding mutation had markedly reduced brain levels of Strumpellin and WASH1, endo-lysosomal abnormalities, cognitive deficits, and progressive motor dysfunction.

checks.claim: Courtland et al. (2021) identified the Ropers et al. (2011) mutation as a homozygous c.3056C-G transversion in the WASHC4 gene, resulting in a pro1019-to-arg (P1019R) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: seven children with homozygous WASHC4c.3056C>G mutations
checks.explanation: c.3056C>G is a transversion giving p.Pro1019Arg as stated in the Introduction.

checks.claim: Courtland et al. (2021) studied 7 children from the family reported by Ropers et al. (2011).
checks.evidence_quote: We retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from seven children with homozygous WASHC4c.3056C>G mutations
checks.explanation: Seven children originally reported by Ropers et al. is supported, but this paper does not state that they all belonged to one family.

checks.claim: Data on the 7 children with homozygous WASHC4 P1019R had been obtained in Oman.
checks.evidence_quote: (obtained by Dr. Rajab in 2010 at the Royal Hospital, Muscat, Oman)

checks.claim: All 7 children with homozygous WASHC4 P1019R had developmental delay or learning difficulties.
checks.evidence_quote: While developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary impetus for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms

checks.claim: All 7 children with homozygous WASHC4 P1019R had motor symptoms, including clumsiness, fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria.
checks.evidence_quote: all patients also exhibited motor symptoms (mean age=10.4 years old, Figure 8H). The patients’ movements were described as ‘clumsy’ with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam

checks.claim: In HEK cells, WASHC4 P1019R mutant SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wildtype SWIP.
checks.evidence_quote: Compared to WT, MUT SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 (IP: 54.8% and 41.4% of WT SWIP, respectively)

checks.claim: Mice carrying the Washc4 mutation corresponding to P1019R had markedly reduced brain levels of Strumpellin and WASH1.
checks.evidence_quote: Western blot analysis of brain lysate from adult homozygous SWIPP1019R mutant mice ... displayed significantly decreased abundance of two WASH complex members, Strumpellin and WASH1

checks.claim: Mice carrying the Washc4 mutation corresponding to P1019R had endo-lysosomal abnormalities.
checks.evidence_quote: These data support the finding that the SWIPP1019R mutation results in both molecular and morphological abnormalities in the endo-lysosomal pathway.

checks.claim: Mice carrying the Washc4 mutation corresponding to P1019R had cognitive deficits.
checks.evidence_quote: MUT mice showed a significant decrease in conditioned freezing to tone presentation compared to their WT littermates
checks.explanation: Cued fear memory deficit; paper concludes cognitive impairment.

checks.claim: Mice carrying the Washc4 mutation corresponding to P1019R had progressive motor dysfunction.
checks.evidence_quote: SWIPP1019R mutant mice display progressive motor dysfunction in association with these subcellular alterations

paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, with syndromic intellectual disability, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous mutations in the WASHC4 gene: a gln442-to-ter (Q442X) stop-gain mutation and an asp1048-to-gly (D1048G) missense mutation. Each mutation was inherited from one parent. Both sisters had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules.

paragraphs.text: In a 34-year-old patient with mild intellectual disability, short stature, and microcephaly, Assoum et al. (2020) identified compound heterozygous missense mutations in the WASHC4 gene: a lys1079-to-arg (K1079R) substitution and a his503-to-arg (H503R) substitution. One mutation was inherited from each parent.

paragraphs.text: In 2 sisters with a syndromic phenotype of dysmorphisms, intellectual disability, profound developmental disorder, and skeletal muscle involvement, Gangfuß et al. (2022) identified a homozygous variant in the WASHC4 gene; the evidence available here does not specify the variant. Proteomic profiling of one patient's fibroblasts showed dysregulation of proteins relevant to maintaining the neuromuscular axis. Immunostaining of her muscle biopsy confirmed dysregulation of proteins needed for normal muscle function.
